title: Floor register: Threshold file
topics: Linked lists, binary trees and search trees
summary: Tree breadth-first traversal. Count the numbers in the result list that are at least k (greater than or equal to k).
descriptionMd:
Your task
Build a result list using Step 1. Then use that list to find the answer in Step 2.

Inputs
root is the top node of a binary tree. Examples list nodes one level at a time, from left to right. null marks a missing child; [] means no tree. Each node stores its number in val. Its left and right links point to children. The runner builds the nodes for you. k is a whole number. Use it as described in the steps below.

Step 1: Build the result list
root is the top node of a binary tree. Each node has a value and up to two children. The root is at depth 0, its children are at depth 1, and so on. Add the values at each depth. Put one sum per depth in the result list, starting at depth 0. Missing children add nothing. An empty tree gives an empty result list.

Step 2: Return the answer
Count the numbers in the result list that are at least k (greater than or equal to k). Return that count. An empty list gives 0.

Write your function
Complete floorRegisterThresholdFile(root, k). Return the answer from Step 2. Do not print it or read keyboard input. In examples, positions (indexes) start at 0 unless a rule says otherwise.

Each card first builds this result list, then asks for a different answer. Start with the first card. The last card also uses position numbers that start at 1.
constraints: 0 <= node count <= 31; null marks a missing child and does not count as a node.
k is a whole number from 1 to 8. Answers fit in a signed 32-bit integer: -2,147,483,648 through 2,147,483,647.
Input numbers have no decimal part. They range from -1,000,000 to 1,000,000. Follow any extra input rules in Step 1.
Linked lists do not loop back to an earlier node. Tree examples list nodes by level; null means a missing child. The runner builds the nodes shown in the examples.
Efficiency goal: time O(n); extra memory, including the result list, O(n). n is the number of nodes. These labels describe how work and memory grow with the input.
hints: Try a small example by hand. Follow Step 1 and write down its result list.

Put one sum per depth in the result list, starting at depth 0. Missing children add nothing. An empty tree gives an empty result list. Keep track of the numbers or places you have already checked.
Count the numbers in the result list that are at least k (greater than or equal to k). Return that count. An empty list gives 0. Check what to do if the result list is empty.

cases.explanation: Step 1 gives the result list [7,-3,7]. Here k = 3. The numbers at least 3 are [7,7]. There are 2, so return 2.

Step 1 gives the result list []. Here k = 1. The numbers at least 1 are []. There are 0, so return 0.
